title: Thread safety and immutability
idea: A class is thread-safe when every caller sees correct results however threads interleave. The cheapest way there is state nobody can change.

analogy.text: A whiteboard in a shared office gets half-erased sums when two people edit at once. A printed notice can be read by everyone; a change means printing a new one.
analogy.breaks: Printing costs paper; new Java objects cost little but still allocate.

points: Races need three things: shared data, mutation, and no coordination. Remove any one.
Check-then-act breaks when another thread changes state between the check and the act.
`synchronized` makes check-and-act atomic; `volatile` shows writes but leaves `n++` non-atomic.
Immutable objects need no lock: final fields, defensive copies, changes return new objects.

hero.title: Two withdrawals race on one balance

messages.label: read 100: is 100 >= 80?
messages.note: A checks the balance. It passes, so A decides to pay out 80.

messages.label: read 100: is 100 >= 80?
messages.note: Before A writes, B checks the same unchanged balance. It also passes.

messages.label: write 100 - 80 = 20
messages.note: B pays out 80. The balance is now 20.

messages.label: write 20 - 80 = -60
messages.note: A acts on its old decision. The wallet pays 160 from 100.

messages.label: lock; check 100; write 20
messages.note: With `synchronized`, A holds the lock from check to write. B cannot check in between.

messages.label: lock; check 20: rejected
messages.note: B checks only after A finishes, sees 20 and is refused. The invariant holds.

code.title: The race, then the lock
code.caption: Latches force the unlucky timing that production hits rarely. The unsafe wallet overpays; the synchronized one cannot.

walk.text: Thread A passes the check, then pauses before writing. Real schedulers do this at random.
Thread B runs a full withdrawal inside A's gap, against the same unchanged balance.
Check and act are two separate steps with nothing guarding the gap between them.
One `synchronized` method makes check and act indivisible; a second caller waits for the lock.
Getters lock too, for visibility. A `volatile` field also gives visibility, but `n++` on it still races.
Whichever thread wins, exactly one withdrawal succeeds, so only counts are printed.

code.title: Immutable value, atomic swap
code.caption: An immutable record shared by four threads. Updates build new objects and swap the reference atomically.

walk.text: The compact constructor validates input and freezes the list with `List.copyOf`.
The caller mutates its own list later; the config kept its own copy.
The accessor returns the unmodifiable copy, so nobody can change state through it.
A change returns a new object. Old snapshots stay valid for any thread reading them.
The only shared mutable thing is one reference, swapped with `updateAndGet`.
After `join`, no update was lost and the first version is untouched.

pitfalls: Making fields `final` but storing the caller's `ArrayList`: the caller can still change your state.
Locking the setter but not the getter: readers on other threads may see stale values.
Treating a record as deeply immutable: a record holding a mutable list is only shallowly immutable.

quiz.q: Four threads each call this 1,000 times on one shared instance. Which statement is true?
options: Possibly under 4000: `n++` is read, add, write
quiz.why: `volatile` makes each write visible, not atomic. `n++` is read, add, write: two threads can read the same value and lose an update.

takeaway: Share nothing mutable; when you must, guard the whole check-then-act with one lock.

starters: How do I make a class with a list field truly immutable?
Why does volatile not fix a lost update on n++?
